content: Secretion refers to the biological process in which cells produce, modify, and release chemical substances. Unlike excretion, the substances secreted often serve specific functions rather than being waste products. Examples of secreted substances include digestive enzymes, gastric acid, and pulmonary surfactant. In humans, as in all eukaryotic cells, secretion is a highly evolved and complex process. Proteins destined for secretion are synthesized by ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER). During synthesis, these proteins are translocated into the ER lumen, where they undergo glycosylation and are assisted in proper folding by molecular chaperones. Misfolded proteins are identified and retrotranslocated to the cytosol via ER-associated degradation, where they are broken down by proteasomes. Properly folded proteins are packaged into vesicles and transported to the Golgi apparatus. Within the Golgi apparatus, the glycosylation of proteins is further modified, and additional post-translational modifications, such as cleavage and functionalization, may occur. The proteins are then sorted into secretory vesicles, which travel along the cytoskeleton to the cell membrane. In some cases, further modifications occur within the secretory vesicles, such as the cleavage of proinsulin into insulin. Finally, the vesicles fuse with the cell membrane in a process called exocytosis, releasing their contents into the extracellular environment. Some proteins, such as fibroblast growth factors (FGF1 and FGF2) and interleukin-1 (IL-1), are secreted through non-classical pathways that do not involve the ER-Golgi system. These proteins lack signal sequences and utilize alternative mechanisms for secretion. Many human cell types function as secretory cells, equipped with well-developed endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus to support their roles in secretion. Secretion is not exclusive to eukaryotic cells; it is also observed in bacteria and archaea. ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are common across all domains of life. The Sec system, a conserved secretion pathway, is homologous to the translocon in the eukaryotic ER and includes the Sec61 complex in yeast and the SecYEG complex in bacteria. In Gram-negative bacteria, secretion is more complex due to the presence of two membranes, necessitating specialized secretion systems. Type I Secretion System The Type I secretion system is similar to ABC transporters but includes additional proteins that form a continuous channel spanning the inner and outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria. This system consists of three protein subunits: the ABC protein, a membrane fusion protein (MFP), and an outer membrane protein (OMP). It transports a variety of molecules, including ions, drugs, and proteins ranging from 20 to 100 kDa in size. Type II Secretion System Proteins secreted via the Type II system rely on the Sec system for initial transport into the periplasm. Once in the periplasm, they pass through the outer membrane via a multimeric complex of secretin proteins. This system involves 10–15 additional inner and outer membrane proteins, many of which have unknown functions. Gram-negative bacteria also use a modified version of the Type II system for the biogenesis of Type IV pili. Type III Secretion System (T3SS) The Type III secretion system is homologous to the basal body of bacterial flagella. Certain bacteria, such as Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia, use this system to inject proteins directly into eukaryotic cells. The system is activated by low calcium concentrations in the cytosol, as demonstrated by the LcrV antigen in Yersinia pestis. In plant pathogens, the Hrp system injects harpins into plant cells through similar mechanisms. This system allows bacteria to deliver toxins directly from their cytoplasm into the host cell cytoplasm. Type IV Secretion System The Type IV secretion system is homologous to bacterial conjugation machinery and is capable of transporting both DNA and proteins. It was first identified in Agrobacterium tumefaciens, which uses this system to transfer the Ti plasmid and proteins into host cells, causing crown gall tumors. Helicobacter pylori uses a Type IV system to inject CagA into gastric epithelial cells, while Bordetella pertussis partially secretes pertussis toxin through this system. Type V Secretion System Also known as the autotransporter system, the Type V secretion system utilizes the Sec system to cross the inner membrane. Proteins using this pathway form a beta-barrel structure with their C-terminus, which inserts into the outer membrane, allowing the rest of the protein (the passenger domain) to be secreted outside the cell. Autotransporters are often cleaved, leaving the beta-barrel domain in the outer membrane and releasing the passenger domain. Some researchers believe remnants of autotransporters may have evolved into porins, which also form beta-barrel structures. Type VI Secretion System The Type VI secretion system has been described in bacteria such as Vibrio cholerae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Proteins secreted by this system lack N-terminal signal sequences. Twin-Arginine Translocation (Tat) Pathway The Tat pathway, used by bacteria, mitochondria, and chloroplasts, transports fully folded proteins across membranes, unlike the Sec-dependent export system. This pathway is named for its requirement of two consecutive arginines in the signal sequence for targeting. Release of Outer Membrane Vesicles Gram-negative bacteria also release material through the formation of outer membrane vesicles. Portions of the outer membrane pinch off, forming spherical structures composed of a lipid bilayer that encloses periplasmic materials. These vesicles can contain virulence factors, exhibit immunomodulatory effects, and directly adhere to and intoxicate host cells.
